title: Teachers as Workers Approved
author: Jacob Allee
summary: Jacob Allee, a curriculum maker and former classical Christian school teacher, responds to a viral claim that AI has made Teachers Pay Teachers and human-made assignments obsolete. He argues that teachers have a duty to be "workers approved", which means mastering the content and curriculum they hand to students rather than using materials as a buffer between themselves and their classes. He compares copied lesson materials to a pastor who downloads sermons, and he insists the problem of disengaged teachers predates AI but is now easier to indulge. His case for buying human-made curriculum rests on the dignity of the people who labored over it, not on the commercial interest he openly admits. He ends by contrasting an education that seeks the shortest and cheapest route to a finish line with one that is a long, costly climb.
points: A teacher need not write all their own curriculum, but must work through and understand whatever they give students, doing the assignments they expect students to do.
Teachers should be modelling the life of a learner, so the gap between their knowledge and their students’ knowledge should widen each year rather than stall.
AI does not create the problem of checked-out teachers but lowers the cost of becoming one, which makes the temptation sharper for those who want to be good.
Choosing human-made curriculum over free AI output is framed as care for the people who produced it, in the same way one would buy a painting from an artist.
The author treats education as long struggle and toil rather than efficient delivery, and that is why shortcuts cost more than they save.
quotes: Teachers don’t have to make all of their own curriculum, but they should be working to become masters of their content and curriculum. It’s not shameful if you didn’t make the curriculum you are using, but it is utterly shameful if you give it to your students without having done your best to work through it and understand it yourself.

We are supposed to be the role-models of what it looks like to be a learner, but too many are checked out, resigned, resting on their laurels, and simply content with the fact that they have “a process that works.” But for a teacher who is worth his salt, the gap between his knowledge and his students’ knowledge should be widening every single year.
I am talking about this because now it is easier than ever for bad teachers to become worse and for good teachers to be relegated to the trash heap as unnecessary and obsolete.
The answers to these questions, respectively, are “because being human matters” and “because human beings matter.

The teachers who use curriculum as a buffer between themselves and their students, the ones who just need content from wherever to keep the kids busy, the ones who don’t study it themselves or push themselves to know more than they teach (or even as much as they “teach”), they are behaving in an inhumane manner.

The mistake of modern education is so often to see the whole process of education as merely finding the shortest and easiest and cheapest route to the finish line, but real education has always been about long journeys, struggle and toil, and it costs us something (financially and personally) because it’s valuable
The goal has never been to simply get things done as quickly and as easily as possible, that is the path to vice, not virtue.
